children.text: June Millington’s narrated voice opens the video before the song’s other performers take over the foreground. Her measured storytelling makes the Bakunawa myth arrive as something already carried in a human voice, so inheritance begins as an act of telling. When other voices enter later, they sound like another stage in the story’s movement across people and generations.

June Millington continues her storytelling, interrupted by flashing of modern performers three times. Once after "Bakunawa, bent snake", once after "moon eater", and finally once after and during "the cause of natural phenomena". The melding of the interruptions is accompanied by sounds of flickering, like film passing through, representing the fusion of the ancestral diaspora with modern art style and retelling.

Cutting away from Ruby as she continues to speak, drawn depictions of the bakunawa are displayed in direct parallel of Ruby's personification of the myth. Similarly, the second drawing depicts what may be Ruby herself, effortlessly weathering the storm.

Ruby raps in tagalog and makes a very deep impact with the translation of the overall verse being that you shouldn't underestimate her, that she is fierce, and that she is the Bakunawa which is a Philippines mythological serpent-like creature also known as the "Moon-Eater." This is evident in her lines like "Ako ang Bakunawa", and "Nakatira sa dilim." These lines translate to "I am the Bakunawa" and "I live in the dark" respectively. These lines give insight to her lyrical inspiration of Bakunawa. I also loved the use of Tagolog and Bisaya as a Filipino-American as it truly feels like there is a connection with her culture and people-alike.

The vocals come in with the chorus and it has a very repetitive but catchy feeling. It also has a very militant and affirming feeling with the adlibs and background vocals backing up the overall declaration that Ruby is the Bakunawa, that she really is the "Moon-eater." She reiterates what she had previously stated in the verse saying "Hoy ako ang Bakunawa! ako ang Bakunawa." Which translates to " Hey I am the Bakunawa! I am the Bakunawa." It also uses a miniscule cultural nods to her Filipina background with the feeling of a small ensemble/use of parasols in the chorus versus her solo sound in the verses.

Officially, this is where Ruby begins rapping away, albeit in her native language. This serves as an introduction about her and her origins, and from her aggressive tone and the angryish faces she makes (alongside the bloodsheed), Ruby is proud of her heritage.

Ibarra uses the phrase “And I was born with two tongues, so I carry two guns,” which represents the power in being born speaking two languages. Words are the most powerful form of communication and tie someone to their ancestry, hence why Ibarra compares it to carrying a gun. Knowing two languages both connects you to the past and the present, myths are carried down from generation to generation.

Ibarra cuts from red to blue lighting, but still maintaining the same look when she begins the next verse, likely signifying the two different sides within her. When she is in red lighting, she calls back to the sun and fire, and in the blue lighting, she weaves in the moon and the ocean. Both are equally significant, but also polar opposites which ties back to Ibarra’s roots and origins.

Ruby Ibarra’s first time rapping in English adds new orchestration and instrumentals that are more intricate. These musical additions mirror the complexity of her identity. She is Filipina American, but addresses the story of the Bakunawa in all of the languages she speaks. Her ability to communicate her memories and stories to different audiences highlights how she holds importance for all of her cultural and community affiliations.

There's no actual music here, but it does introduce us to the song as a clearly political and suggestive song. The imagery of the actual video gives us the notion that these issues have been issues for a long time. A seemingly old and fragile woman in a rocking chair talking about the stories behind the meaning of the song.

I absolutely love this little breakdown section. I thought all the instruments came together really well after that massive build up. The vocal mixing is wonderful, and the bassline really gets you wanting to dance. The rhythm and groove is a pretty funky fun beat that I love, and makes the message even more powerful.

In this section, we get a prologue before the song starts. The prologue is in English, letting the audience who don't speak Tagalog understand what the Bakunawa is. However, once the music starts playing, we no longer get English lyrics. This forces the English audience to remain curious about what the Bakunawa is and keeps it authentic to the culture. The music and visuals themselves, however, are powerful enough to help the audience understand what the Bakunawa is. Going back to the prologue, the audience gets a glimpse of a natural phenomenon.

The candles turn off, and the music starts to get quieter. Ruby starts singing/rapping in a speaking manner, and this time in English. The way she speaks sounds like a chant. Ruby's voice is powerful, strong, and brave. With both the mixture of her tone of voice plus the lyrics, Ruby makes it clear she is speaking out about cultural erasure, breaking generational cycles, and resistance through the metaphor of Bakunawa.

As Ruby raps, her words and her breaths are short and her words feel like strict, strong stomps that match the precise drum beat in the background. This represents how her memory of herself in America was stripped of its whimsy and dynamism, reduced to something static and rigid. The quick and rigid raps begin to quicken, depicting how the pressure to assimilate to the “American norm” was a stressful memory and she wanted to escape to show and live her life not being afraid or held back from showing her culture.

Immediately after our introduction to the legend of the Bakunawa, the instrumentals blend into a mixture featuring vocals, modern/electronic percussive elements, and even some rattling that eludes to the serpent. There are definitely some moments where the beat in concentrated, but the intensity remains somewhat restrained. The lyrics, I find, in this section from our singer builds the foundation for the remainder of the song; as she recounts making it through the battle of the night, she poses it as a question to the listener, asking it as an invitation for internal reflection.

Ibarra here choses to use a very compressed voice in layer with heavy background vocals to support the compression. In this section, it instantly brings the audience into the mistery of a culture that we do not know. It is also trying to tell the story that in order to understand their culture, we need to dive deep in and set our mood to match.

By paneling away from the frame that Ibarra is showing of pregnancy, it shows the symbol of rebirth and giving us more context about the my of Bakunawa. It also allows the audience to understand that in Philipino culture, rebirth is the key, and they always stay strong even after they die. They find ways to come back to the world through rebirth and carrying what they have in their culture while passing it on.

This is when the instrumentation changes again back to what is similar to my previous annotation. There is droning in the background with quiet but edgy instrumentation. There are no vocals at first; then they come back in, more speech-like than previously. I think this is to put an emphasis on the message they want to leave us with.

At this moment, Ibarra shifts out of English for the first time in the song. This linguistic change comes alongside a change in energy as she raps the lyrics instead of singing. These differences combine to suggest that Ibarra may be protecting aspects of intergenerational, cultural memory, as the audience must make an effort to move away from a white/English-centric hegemony to be able to understand her lyrics and access what she says.

This section of the song takes on more layering, as the instrumentals become denser in tandem with multiple voices. The shared voices expressing the story of Bakunawa serve to emphasize the intergenerational nature of how stories are passed along. Instead of one individual passing along the memory to the next generation in a unidirectional way, shared memory becomes something that is created by multiple generations working together.

At this moment, I noticed a change in the voice, rhythm, and intensity. This shift makes the song feel like it moves between different generations and parts of family history. The change from a more personal voice to a stronger rap style makes the memory feel more active and alive. For me, the music shows how memories can change as they move through diaspora and between generations.

In this moment, I notice how the repetition of the words and musical patterns creates a feeling of remembering and returning to the same story. The repeated phrases make the memory feel like something that is carried and repeated over time. The instruments also create a background around the voice, so the personal story feels connected to something larger.

In this segment, the lyrics discuss reclaiming the term and making it something that resonates with her. At this same time I notice a white umbrella appears after there was a previous sea of black umbrellas. In my opinion, the color white symbolizes something pure or the start of something new. So this arrival of the white umbrella can show her reclaiming the term and making it represent her new story rather than the past which were the black umbrellas.

Here the artist speaks about her people's history and then goes on to see there is revolution in her panning to her being pregnant. This again can symbolize how she is the start of a new history of this history and term. Physically with her baby and metaphorically talking about rebirthing the new moon.
Many people with black umbrellas appear on set, showing the people of the nation banding together.
The sudden change in rhythym to a pulsing bass drum and shift out of English propels the song to a new character and direction

The background singers and intense percussion drop out, revealing one lasting voice. This simple descending melody allows for Ibarra to shift her intense rapping style into a more calming form of spoken poetry. This drastic change in rapping style feels more personal and almost as if she's speaking directly to the listener.

As Ibarra sings about red and blue, the lighting of the scene changes to those colors as well. The red seems like the power of the sun while the blue, the power of the moon or the monsoon which she mentions in rap as metaphors for her power as the bakunawa. Visuals from earlier in the MV appear to suggest that she became the bakunawa after being thrown into the sea.

Ibarra mentions wanting to rewrite her story and praying the moon but getting caught, while her shadowed figure apears in front of a gold and then light blue background. Perhaps this implies that she gained her power of the bakunawa from the moon and consequently had to forget her past as a human.

The music transitions from the older woman (June Millington) singing to Ruby Ibarra's rapping with a very firm, declarative style. Her diction and tone forces the viewer to concentrate despite a possible language barrier. Not understanding Tagalog, I felt compelled to find a translation to better understand her message and the conviction with which she is rapping.

This is when the song travels back to Millington. I believe it was an intentional choice by Ibarra to include an older Filipina, as they are the generation that pass down myths, such as that of the Bakunawa, to younger generations. The lyrics "Do you know your story? Why do you feel that pain" signify the specific experiences her generation went through, and carrying on that knowledge down generations is important to her identity.

In the video, which begins with the voice of an old woman, the raw and rough camera movements, the scene of a shaking chair, and the unusual use of focus create a sense of anxiety and tension, as if building up to the introduction of something enormous. In particular, the shots focusing on the woman’s mouth stand out as a visual device that helps the viewer become more immersed in the parts of the story that are meant to be emphasized.

As the angular braided hair extends beyond the frame, it creates a strong sense of vitality, as if it is constantly receiving energy from somewhere outside the screen. Combined with hands that resemble those of an alien creature, it seems to convey, together with the rap, an unstoppable and powerful life force through nonverbal elements.

The singer picture is seated as she raps about her history and her future as she confirms her identity with the nicknames she gives herself, "mooneater," and such. This is cut between animations showing her "fight," giving a strong sense of connectivity, evoking a storyteller and her paper puppets to tell of this story.
